title: How to do well in a German job interview
description: What to expect in a German interview process, how to prepare, how to talk about your visa status and which cultural details make a difference.
html:
An interview invitation means your application has already worked. What follows is a process that is more structured and more direct than in many countries, and knowing the pattern removes most of the nerves. Here is how German interviews tend to run and how to prepare.

The process

Most companies run two to three rounds: a short phone or video screening with HR, an interview with the hiring manager and often a technical task or case, and sometimes a final conversation with a senior manager. The whole process takes two to six weeks. You will usually be told the timeline, and it is fine to ask.

Which language

If the job was advertised in English, the interview will be in English. If it was advertised in German, expect German, possibly with a switch to English for technical parts. Be honest about your level; interviewers can tell, and they respect a candidate who says "my German is B1 and I am taking classes" more than one who struggles through.

Preparation

Research the company properly: products, recent news, the team you would join. Reread the job description and prepare an example for each requirement. Prepare three questions of your own. Test your video setup. Arrive, or log in, five minutes early; punctuality is read as respect.

Talking about your visa

Raise it before they do. One clear sentence is enough: "I hold an Opportunity Card, so I can start immediately and the company only needs to confirm the contract for my residence permit." Employers are far more relaxed about visa status when the candidate clearly understands the process.

Cultural details

Use surnames and the formal address until invited otherwise. Answer questions directly; long detours read as evasion. Modesty is fine, but state your achievements plainly and with numbers. Small talk is short. Interruptions are rare, so wait for the interviewer to finish.

Common questions

Why this company, why this role, why Germany. Walk me through your CV. Describe a project that went wrong and what you learned. Where do you see yourself in five years. What are your salary expectations; have a number ready, based on research, and give a range. And, almost always: do you have any questions for us. Have them ready.
